notes: The horse colors are retained without assigning them symbolic meanings that the vision does not explain.
These public verses correspond to Hebrew 2:1–4; all original source records are retained in the audit binding.
vocabulary: Return
The repeated verb connects the people’s return to the LORD with his return to them.
Horns
Images of the powers that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.

notes: This public chapter begins at Hebrew 2:5; the difference is numbering, not missing text.
“After glory” is a difficult expression. “His eye” preserves the Hebrew pronoun; the image marks preciousness and vulnerability.
The passage shifts between the LORD speaking and a speaker sent by the LORD. The pronouns are retained without forcing a single explanation.
vocabulary: Measuring cord
A builder’s instrument used here in a vision of Jerusalem’s future.
Wall of fire
The LORD’s own protection pictured around an unwalled city.

notes: “The accuser” renders the role expressed by the Hebrew satan in this courtroom scene.
The Hebrew says “I said.” The prophet’s intervention is retained rather than reassigned to the angel.
The one stone and seven eyes are preserved as the vision presents them; their full symbolism is not specified.
vocabulary: Burning stick
A piece of burning wood rescued from a fire.
Branch
A growth image used as a title of the coming servant.

notes: The lamp-and-channel arrangement is difficult. The draft keeps the repeated seven without claiming a fully reconstructable design.
The repeated cry “Grace, grace” is retained; it can also express a wish for favor or blessing upon the stone.
The Hebrew calls the object a tin stone, commonly understood as a plumb weight. The seven eyes range over the earth.
The flowing substance is literally “gold.” The two “anointed ones” are literally “sons of oil”; the translation does not name the figures.
vocabulary: Spirit
The LORD’s enabling presence, contrasted with military might and human strength.
Plumb stone
A suspended weight used to establish a vertical line.

notes: The clauses about the two offenses and the scroll’s sides are difficult. Their relation to the curse is clearer than the exact construction.
“Appearance” follows the pinned Hebrew; it is not changed to “iniquity.”
vocabulary: Cubit
An ancient length measure based on the forearm; the scroll is twenty by ten cubits.
Ephah
A grain measure and its measuring container, which becomes the vision’s basket.

notes: The Hebrew can mean “winds” or “spirits.” The four are presented as going out from the Lord’s presence.
The white horses go after the black ones in the pinned wording; the direction is not changed to west.
“Crowns” is plural and Joshua is named. Verse 13 speaks of counsel between two; verse 14’s Helem and Hen are not silently harmonized with Heldai and Josiah in verse 10.
vocabulary: Branch
The title joins building the temple, rule, and the relationship with priesthood.
Memorial
Something retained to keep people or events in remembrance.

notes: Bethel is understood here as the community sending the delegation; the Hebrew can also be construed with Bethel as part of a personal name.
The commands pair faithful love with concrete treatment of the widow, orphan, foreigner, and poor person.
vocabulary: Fast
Abstaining from food as part of mourning or religious observance.
Flint
An image of extreme hardness in the refusal to hear.

notes: The naming of Jerusalem and the mountain describes their restored character; it does not rename every earlier occurrence.
The four fast months remain distinct even as their observance is transformed into joy.
vocabulary: Faithfulness and righteousness
Terms describing the reliability and rightness of the restored relationship.
Garment corner
The edge grasped in the image of people seeking to accompany a Judean.

notes: The clause about humanity’s eye and the LORD is difficult; the draft retains the eye image rather than replacing it with an inferred meaning.
The term for the people settling in Ashdod can suggest mixed or illegitimate descent; its precise social sense here is uncertain.
“Saved” preserves the Hebrew passive form; “victorious” is another contextual rendering. Matthew 21 quotes only part of this verse.
The slingstone image and the final “its” are difficult. The draft does not supply a fully certain referent or reconstruct the scene.
vocabulary: Blood of your covenant
Blood marking the covenant relationship invoked in the release of prisoners.
Bow
Judah and Ephraim are pictured as weapons readied for action.

notes: The subject of the passage through the sea of distress is not fully explicit. The draft preserves the singular movement without naming a new actor.
vocabulary: Household gods (teraphim)
Household cult objects associated here with deceptive guidance.
Cornerstone; tent peg
Images of stable support joined to images of leadership and strength.

notes: “Afflicted” follows the pinned Hebrew rather than a reconstruction referring to sheep merchants.
“Potter” follows the Hebrew wording. The thirty pieces of silver and the house of the LORD remain explicit.
vocabulary: Favor; Bonds
Names of the two staffs; their breaking gives the action its symbolic force.
Worthless shepherd
A leader condemned for abandoning the flock.

notes: The Hebrew shifts from “me, whom they pierced” to mourning “for him.” Both pronouns are retained; the draft does not remove the tension.
Hadad-rimmon and Megiddo locate a comparison whose precise historical reference is not explained here.
vocabulary: Cup of reeling
An image of destabilizing intoxication for those surrounding Jerusalem.
Only child; firstborn
Family losses used to express the intensity of mourning.

notes: The statement about being bought from youth is difficult; the draft preserves it without inventing an occupation history.
The wounds are literally “between your arms,” potentially the chest or back area. “Those who love me” is retained without assigning this exchange to a later figure.
vocabulary: Fountain
The opened water source is an image of cleansing from sin and impurity.
Refine
Purifying metal by fire becomes an image for testing the surviving people.

notes: The capture of the city includes rape. The draft names the harm plainly.
The pinned wording describes fleeing and ends “with you.” These are not silently changed to an alternative verb or to “with him.”
The written form is rendered with the congealing verb; the source also records a reading tradition involving frost. The whole light-and-cold clause is difficult.
Verse 14 can mean fighting at or against Jerusalem. Verse 18 has an elliptical negative; “rain” is supplied from verse 17. “Canaanite” in verse 21 may also mean a merchant.
vocabulary: Living waters
Flowing water, here issuing from Jerusalem in both seasons.
Festival of Booths
The festival named in the vision of the nations’ worship.
